claim: Blue light activation of the epidermis alone can produce action potentials in SA1 fiber types in mice expressing channelrhodopsin (ChR2) in keratinocytes.
source: Using mice expressing channelrhodopsin (ChR2) in keratinocytes we show that blue light activation of the epidermis alone can produce action potentials (APs) in multiple types of cutaneous sensory neurons including SA1, A-HTMR, CM, CH, CMC, CMH and CMHC fiber types.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from experiments using ChR2-expressing keratinocyte mice.

claim: Intrinsic sensory transduction mechanisms in epidermal keratinocytes can directly elicit action potential firing in nociceptive sensory afferents.
source: These findings support the idea that intrinsic sensory transduction mechanisms in epidermal keratinocytes can directly elicit AP firing in nociceptive as well as tactile sensory afferents and suggest a significantly expanded role for the epidermis in sensory processing.
evidence: The abstract concludes this based on the experimental findings presented.

evidence: The abstract concludes this based on the experimental findings presented.

claim: The skin produces neuroactive substances that are postulated to directly and indirectly modulate the activity of sensory fibers.
source: In response to stimuli, the skin produces neuroactive substances that are postulated to directly and indirectly modulate the activity of sensory fibers (Groneberg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The skin produces glutamate as a neuroactive substance.
source: These substances include glutamate (Nordlind et al., 1993; Fischer et al., 2009), ATP (Cook and McCleskey, 2002; Inoue et al., 2005; Dussor et al., 2009; Barr et al., 2013), acetylcholine (ACh) (Grando et al., 1993; Wessler et al., 1998), epinephrine (Khasar et al., 1999; Pullar et al., 2006), CGRP (Hou et al., 2011), neurotrophic growth factors (Truzzi et al., 2011) and cytokines (Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The skin expresses ligand-gated ion channels including glutamate, ATP, nicotinic, muscarinic, 5-hydroxytryptamine, glycine and gamma-aminobutyric receptors.
source: The skin also expresses ligand-gated (glutamate, ATP, nicotinic, muscarinic, 5-hydroxytryptamine, glycine and gamma-aminobutyric) and voltage-gated (sodium, calcium, transient receptor potential [TRP], potassium and cyclic nucleotide) ion channels and growth factor and cytokine receptors (Olah et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The skin expresses voltage-gated ion channels including sodium, calcium, transient receptor potential (TRP), potassium and cyclic nucleotide channels.
source: The skin also expresses ligand-gated (glutamate, ATP, nicotinic, muscarinic, 5-hydroxytryptamine, glycine and gamma-aminobutyric) and voltage-gated (sodium, calcium, transient receptor potential [TRP], potassium and cyclic nucleotide) ion channels and growth factor and cytokine receptors (Olah et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The skin expresses growth factor and cytokine receptors.
source: The skin also expresses ligand-gated (glutamate, ATP, nicotinic, muscarinic, 5-hydroxytryptamine, glycine and gamma-aminobutyric) and voltage-gated (sodium, calcium, transient receptor potential [TRP], potassium and cyclic nucleotide) ion channels and growth factor and cytokine receptors (Olah et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Complex autocrine and paracrine signaling between epithelial and neural tissues underlie sensory signaling.
source: The expression of neuroactivators and voltage and ion-gated channels indicates that complex autocrine and paracrine signaling between epithelial and neural tissues underlie sensory signaling (Conti-Fine et al., 2000; Peier et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2008; Atoyan et al., 2009; Dussor et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the expression patterns, with supporting citations.

claim: Non-neuronal cells of the skin, specifically keratinocytes, contribute to the initial transduction process through regulated release of neuroactive substances.
source: It has been proposed that non-neuronal cells of the skin, specifically keratinocytes, contribute to the initial transduction process through regulated release of neuroactive substances (Zhao et al., 2008; Dussor et al., 2009; Mandadi et al., 2009; Hou et al., 2011; Barr et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a proposal from the literature with supporting citations.

claim: Blue light stimulation of the skin of transgenic rats that expressed ChR2 in primary afferents under the Thy-1.2 promoter exhibited nocifensive type responses.
source: For example, Ji and colleagues (Ji et al., 2012) showed that blue light stimulation of the skin of transgenic rats that expressed ChR2 in primary afferents under the Thy-1.2 promoter exhibited nocifensive type responses.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: Light-induced behavioral sensitivity was observed in mice in which the Nav1.8 promoter drove expression of ChR2 in a subset of primary afferents.
source: Similarly, Daou et al. (Daou et al., 2013) showed light-induced behavioral sensitivity in mice in which the Nav1.8 promoter drove expression of ChR2 in a subset of primary afferents.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: Blue light stimulation of isolated skin with ChR2 expressed in Merkel cells elicited action potential trains in slowly adapting type 1 (SA1) afferents.
source: In another optogenetic model, Maksimovic and colleagues directed ChR2 expression to the non-neuronal Merkel cells of the epidermis. Using an ex vivo electrophysiologic preparation they showed that blue light stimulation of the isolated skin elicited AP trains in slowly adapting type 1 (SA1) afferents, thus confirming the essential transducer role of Merkel cells in transmission of mechanical stimuli by SA1 tactile afferents.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study by Maksimovic and colleagues.

claim: Merkel cells have an essential transducer role in transmission of mechanical stimuli by SA1 tactile afferents.
source: In another optogenetic model, Maksimovic and colleagues directed ChR2 expression to the non-neuronal Merkel cells of the epidermis. Using an ex vivo electrophysiologic preparation they showed that blue light stimulation of the isolated skin elicited AP trains in slowly adapting type 1 (SA1) afferents, thus confirming the essential transducer role of Merkel cells in transmission of mechanical stimuli by SA1 tactile afferents.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the cited study by Maksimovic and colleagues.

claim: Light stimulation of the skin and activation of ChR2 in sensory afferents elicits robust nocifensive behaviors in mice.
source: Similar to Daou et al. (Daou et al., 2013), we found that light stimulation of the skin and activation of ChR2 in sensory afferents elicits robust nocifensive behaviors in mice.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study, with reference to a similar finding by Daou et al.

claim: Light stimulation of mice that only express ChR2 in skin keratinocytes is sufficient to generate nocifensive behaviors.
source: Remarkably, for mice that only express ChR2 in skin keratinocytes, light stimulation was also sufficient to generate nocifensive behaviors and regulate firing properties and evoke APs in specific subsets of cutaneous afferents, several which are known to activate in response to painful stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: Light stimulation of mice that only express ChR2 in skin keratinocytes regulates firing properties and evokes action potentials in specific subsets of cutaneous afferents.
source: Remarkably, for mice that only express ChR2 in skin keratinocytes, light stimulation was also sufficient to generate nocifensive behaviors and regulate firing properties and evoke APs in specific subsets of cutaneous afferents, several which are known to activate in response to painful stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: Expression of the chloride pump NpHR3.0 in keratinocytes significantly reduced action potential firing in cutaneous afferents.
source: In addition, expression of the chloride pump NpHR3.0 in keratinocytes significantly reduced AP firing in cutaneous afferents.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: Merkel cells are not unique in their ability to directly generate action potentials in sensory neurons.
source: These data indicate that Merkel cells are not unique in their ability to directly generate action potentials in sensory neurons and that light-mediated activation of keratinocytes is sufficient to engage an endogenous mechanism that can directly regulate cutaneous afferent firing.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Light-mediated activation of keratinocytes is sufficient to engage an endogenous mechanism that can directly regulate cutaneous afferent firing.
source: These data indicate that Merkel cells are not unique in their ability to directly generate action potentials in sensory neurons and that light-mediated activation of keratinocytes is sufficient to engage an endogenous mechanism that can directly regulate cutaneous afferent firing.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: 200 characterized cutaneous afferents were recorded from in the electrophysiological experiments (86 C-fibers, 37 Aδ, 77 Aβ).
source: In these electrophysiological experiments we have recorded from 200 characterized cutaneous afferents (86 C-fibers, 37 Aδ, 77 Aβ) from the three different mouse genotypes (49 Prph-ChR2, 80 KRT-ChR2, 71 KRT-NpHR).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the experimental data.

claim: Recordings were obtained from three different mouse genotypes: 49 Prph-ChR2, 80 KRT-ChR2, and 71 KRT-NpHR.
source: In these electrophysiological experiments we have recorded from 200 characterized cutaneous afferents (86 C-fibers, 37 Aδ, 77 Aβ) from the three different mouse genotypes (49 Prph-ChR2, 80 KRT-ChR2, 71 KRT-NpHR).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the experimental data.

claim: Aδ-HTMRs had mechanical thresholds ranging from 5 to 100 mN with a mean of 26.7 mN.

claim: No significant differences in mechanical, heat, and cold threshold values were observed between genotypes.
source: No significant differences in these values were observed between genotypes.

claim: All Prph-ChR2 mice (5 out of 5 mice tested) demonstrated robust light-induced tail-flick or hindpaw withdrawal in <30 ms in response to a 473 nm laser light flash.
source: Behaviorally, all Prph-ChR2 mice (5 out of 5 mice tested) demonstrated robust light-induced tail-flick or hindpaw withdrawal in <30 ms in response to a 473 nm laser light flash, consistent with previous findings (Grando et al., 1993; Daou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a behavioral finding from the experiments.

claim: Wildtype littermate mice (n = 5) were unresponsive to 473 nm laser light flash.
source: Wildtype littermate mice (n = 5) were unresponsive.
evidence: This is stated as a control finding from the experiments.

claim: ChR2 neurons in Prph-ChR2 mice responded to blue light pulses ranging from 39.7 mW (5–10,000 ms) to 0.7 mW (1000 ms pulse).
source: ChR2 neurons responded to blue light pulses ranging from 39.7 mW (5–10,000 ms) to 0.7 mW (1000 ms pulse).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Recordings were made from 49 characterized sensory neurons from 7 Prph-ChR2 mice with 26 responders that included 1 A-fiber and 25 C-fiber nociceptors.
source: Recordings were made from 49 characterized sensory neurons from 7 mice with 26 responders that included 1 A-fiber and 25 C-fiber nociceptors (identified based on their response to noxious mechanical or thermal stimuli) (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Among laser-responsive C-fibers in Prph-ChR2 mice, 21 responded to mechanical stimuli.
source: Among laser-responsive C-fibers, 21 responded to mechanical stimuli and of these, 14 responded to heat and/or cold stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Among laser-responsive C-fibers in Prph-ChR2 mice that responded to mechanical stimuli, 14 responded to heat and/or cold stimuli.
source: Among laser-responsive C-fibers, 21 responded to mechanical stimuli and of these, 14 responded to heat and/or cold stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Four laser-responsive C-fibers in Prph-ChR2 mice were classified as responding only to heat stimulation.
source: Four were classified as responding only to heat stimulation and 7 responded only to mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Seven laser-responsive C-fibers in Prph-ChR2 mice responded only to mechanical stimuli.
source: Four were classified as responding only to heat stimulation and 7 responded only to mechanical stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Peak instantaneous frequencies were significantly higher for suprathreshold mechanical stimulation compared to light stimulation in Prph-ChR2 mechanically responsive C-fibers, averaging 33.9 Hz for mechanical vs 8.6 Hz for light stimulation (@ 39.7 mW).
source: Peak instantaneous frequencies (IF) were significantly higher for suprathreshold mechanical stimulation, averaging 33.9 Hz for mechanical vs 8.6 Hz for light stimulation (@ 39.7 mW) for all mechanically responsive C-fibers.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The average peak instantaneous frequency seen with laser light in Prph-ChR2 mice was similar to that seen in polymodal nociceptors in response to noxious heat.
source: Interestingly, the average peak IF seen with laser light was similar to that seen in polymodal nociceptors (the majority of cutaneous afferents) in response to noxious heat (McIlwrath et al., 2007; Lawson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous findings with citations.

claim: Afferent-expressed ChR2 activation can evoke a 'baseline' response of putative nociceptors that reflects the intrinsic properties of these cells.
source: This raised the possibility that afferent-expressed ChR2 activation can evoke a 'baseline' response of putative nociceptors that reflects the intrinsic properties of these cells and that more naturalistic responses require collaboration of surrounding cells, including keratinocytes.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility raised by the data.

claim: More naturalistic responses in nociceptors require collaboration of surrounding cells, including keratinocytes.
source: This raised the possibility that afferent-expressed ChR2 activation can evoke a 'baseline' response of putative nociceptors that reflects the intrinsic properties of these cells and that more naturalistic responses require collaboration of surrounding cells, including keratinocytes.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility raised by the data.

claim: KRT-ChR2 mice exhibited robust expression of ChR2 in epidermal keratinocytes and hair follicles of hairy skin.
source: KRT-ChR2 mice exhibited robust expression of ChR2 in epidermal keratinocytes and hair follicles of hairy skin and basal and suprabasal keratinocytes of glabrous skin (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: KRT-ChR2 mice exhibited robust expression of ChR2 in basal and suprabasal keratinocytes of glabrous skin.
source: KRT-ChR2 mice exhibited robust expression of ChR2 in epidermal keratinocytes and hair follicles of hairy skin and basal and suprabasal keratinocytes of glabrous skin (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ChR2 expression does not occur in dermal vasculature, muscle, or in the DRG of KRT-ChR2 mice.
source: ChR2 expression does not occur in other dermal structures (vasculature, muscle) or in the DRG (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: KRT-ChR2 mice exhibited behavioral responses to blue light stimulation.
source: KRT-ChR2 mice also exhibited behavioral responses to blue light stimulation (Figure 2B, Table 1), but at lower frequencies and with greater latencies relative to Prph-ChR2 mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: KRT-ChR2 mice exhibited behavioral responses to blue light stimulation at lower frequencies and with greater latencies relative to Prph-ChR2 mice.
source: KRT-ChR2 mice also exhibited behavioral responses to blue light stimulation (Figure 2B, Table 1), but at lower frequencies and with greater latencies relative to Prph-ChR2 mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: The average withdrawal latency for KRT-ChR2 mice was 15.75 s ± 2.26 (SEM).
source: The average withdrawal latency for KRT-ChR2 mice was 15.75 s ± 2.26 (SEM) (see Video 1), compared to the millisecond withdrawal responses exhibited by Prph-ChR2 mice.
evidence: This is stated as a behavioral measurement.

claim: All KRT-ChR2 mice responded at least one time out of 10 trials with laser stimulation restricted to a 30 s maximum.
source: Testing was done in a blinded manner and all KRT-ChR2 mice responded at least one time out of 10 trials with laser stimulation restricted to a 30 s maximum.
evidence: This is stated as a behavioral finding.

claim: Laser stimulation of human skin using a thermistor showed a slight increase in surface temperature from 27.5°C to 30.5°C over the 30 s stimulation period.
source: Measures on human skin using a thermistor showed a slight laser-induced increase in surface temperature (from 27.5°C to 30.5°C) over the 30 s stimulation period, indicating that KRT-ChR2 mouse responses were not due to laser heating of the skin.
evidence: This is stated as a control measurement.

claim: KRT-ChR2 mouse responses to blue light were not due to laser heating of the skin.
source: Measures on human skin using a thermistor showed a slight laser-induced increase in surface temperature (from 27.5°C to 30.5°C) over the 30 s stimulation period, indicating that KRT-ChR2 mouse responses were not due to laser heating of the skin.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the control measurement.

claim: Light activation of ChR2-keratinocytes can evoke nocifensive-type behaviors.
source: That light activation of ChR2-keratinocytes could evoke nocifensive-type behaviors suggested that robust communication occurs between keratinocytes and sensory afferents that transmit nociceptive stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the behavioral data.

claim: Robust communication occurs between keratinocytes and sensory afferents that transmit nociceptive stimuli.
source: That light activation of ChR2-keratinocytes could evoke nocifensive-type behaviors suggested that robust communication occurs between keratinocytes and sensory afferents that transmit nociceptive stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the behavioral data.

claim: All 11 ChR2-YFP keratinocytes recorded from KRT-ChR2 mice showed inward current in response to a brief (1 s) flash of blue light.
source: Recordings from 11 ChR2-YFP keratinocytes all showed inward current in response to a brief (1 s) flash of blue light (peak current: median 26.3 pA; steady current: 16.5 pA) (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from patch clamp recordings and shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The median peak current in ChR2-YFP keratinocytes in response to blue light was 26.3 pA.
source: Recordings from 11 ChR2-YFP keratinocytes all showed inward current in response to a brief (1 s) flash of blue light (peak current: median 26.3 pA; steady current: 16.5 pA) (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from patch clamp recordings and shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The median steady current in ChR2-YFP keratinocytes in response to blue light was 16.5 pA.
source: Recordings from 11 ChR2-YFP keratinocytes all showed inward current in response to a brief (1 s) flash of blue light (peak current: median 26.3 pA; steady current: 16.5 pA) (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from patch clamp recordings and shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: No light-induced currents were recorded in keratinocytes cultured from wildtype mice (n = 4 cells).
source: No light-induced currents were recorded in keratinocytes cultured from wildtype mice (n = 4 cells).
evidence: This is stated as a control finding from patch clamp recordings.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings were obtained from 80 cells isolated from 16 KRT-ChR2 mice.
source: Electrophysiological recordings were obtained from 80 cells isolated from 16 KRT-ChR2 mice (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Laser activation induced action potentials in 6 out of 24 unmyelinated nociceptive fiber neurons in KRT-ChR2 mice.
source: Laser activation induced APs in 6 out of 24 unmyelinated nociceptive fiber neurons (Figure 2C,D) and in 4 out of 14 myelinated high-threshold mechanoreceptors (HTMRs) (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from electrophysiological recordings and shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Laser activation induced action potentials in 4 out of 14 myelinated high-threshold mechanoreceptors (HTMRs) in KRT-ChR2 mice.
source: Laser activation induced APs in 6 out of 24 unmyelinated nociceptive fiber neurons (Figure 2C,D) and in 4 out of 14 myelinated high-threshold mechanoreceptors (HTMRs) (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Responses in heat-sensitive neurons in KRT-ChR2 mice are not due to laser-generated heat, as measures using a thermistor show minimal rise (∼1 °C) in temperature over the 5 s recording interval.
source: These responses in heat-sensitive neurons are not due to laser-generated heat, as measures using a thermistor show minimal rise (∼1 °C) in temperature over the 5 s recording interval.
evidence: This is stated as a control measurement and conclusion.

claim: Three myelinated HTMR fibers in KRT-ChR2 mice exhibited apparent summation when the laser was presented with natural stimuli.
source: In addition, 3 myelinated HTMR fibers exhibited apparent summation when the laser was presented with natural stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: In 12 of 18 C-fiber nociceptors from KRT-ChR2 mice, combined laser and natural stimulation evoked significantly more action potentials than natural stimuli alone (p < 0.01 paired T-test, n = 12).
source: In 12 of these fibers, combined laser and natural stimulation evoked significantly more APs than natural stimuli alone (p < 0.01 paired T-test, n = 12) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from electrophysiological recordings with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Six C-fiber nociceptors from KRT-ChR2 mice did not display any summation when pairing laser and natural stimuli.
source: The remaining 6 C-fiber nociceptors did not display any summation when pairing laser and natural stimuli (not shown).
